title: Anselm (1033–1109)
hook: faith seeking understanding, and God as that than which nothing greater can be thought

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Peace of God: councils drawing a line around the defenseless. Your line was truce of god. Did you keep your small truce? Today, a monk who thinks his way toward God. Day eight hundred.

A monk at the abbey of Bec has already written one book about God, a long chain of arguments. Now he wants something shorter: one single argument that needs nothing else to stand on. He hunts for it, and it slips away. He decides the hunt is a distraction and tries to stop, and the thought won't leave him alone. Then, he says, it came. He wrote it up as a prayer, and he tested it against a line monks sang in choir, in the Douay-Rheims: "The fool hath said in his heart: There is no God." Today's word is the monk: Anselm.
screen: `ONE ARGUMENT, NOTHING ELSE NEEDED.` → `IT WOULDN'T LEAVE HIM ALONE.` → `THE FOOL HATH SAID IN HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: Start with the motto. In the preface to the book, the Proslogion, Anselm says he first gave it the title faith seeking understanding. The order matters. In the opening chapter he says, in effect: I don't seek to understand so that I may believe; I believe so that I may understand. Faith is where he starts. Then it goes looking. Next, the name. Anselm offers one for God: that than which nothing greater can be thought. Then he turns to the fool. When the fool hears those words, he understands them, so the idea is at least in his mind. But, Anselm reasons, if it were only in the mind, you could think of something greater: the same thing, existing in reality too. So it must exist in both. Then, the answer. A monk named Gaunilo wrote back on the fool's behalf. By that logic, he said, I could prove a perfect island exists just by picturing one. Anselm wrote a reply, and the objection and the reply are still read with the book. Catholic thinkers have weighed the argument differently; Thomas Aquinas, later, did not accept it as a proof. Finally, the surprise. A few chapters on, Anselm goes further. God, he says, is not only that than which nothing greater can be thought, but something greater than can be thought at all. The book that reaches toward God with careful logic arrives at the edge of the mind and says so. For Anselm, that wasn't defeat. It was the point. That's today's line: faith seeking understanding.
screen: `I BELIEVE SO THAT I MAY UNDERSTAND.` · `NOTHING GREATER CAN BE THOUGHT.` · `GAUNILO AND THE PERFECT ISLAND.` · `GREATER THAN CAN BE THOUGHT.` · then, large: `FAITH SEEKING UNDERSTANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about God, on purpose, for the length of the sit. Not to win an argument. Take Anselm's phrase and turn it slowly: that than which nothing greater can be thought. Try to think of something greater. Notice where your mind runs out. If you pray, let the thinking turn into prayer whenever it wants to, the way Anselm's book does. If you don't, treat it as a puzzle worth two minutes of your attention. If you'd like a third minute, keep going after the bell. The bell holds the time.
Anselm. A monk and teacher who called his book faith seeking understanding, and named God that than which nothing greater can be thought. Today's word.
Your line: faith seeking understanding. Today, take one thing you hold to be true and ask it one honest question. Let the question walk with you. Day eight hundred.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Anselm as a Doctor of the Church, and his motto, faith seeking understanding, is often used to describe the work of theology; students still read his Proslogion in philosophy and theology classes.

he said the reverse: he believed so that he might understand.
Anselm's argument answers a line in the Psalms
he tests it against the fool who hath said in his heart: there is no God.

fork.setup: you've written a short book reasoning toward God. a fellow monk writes back saying your argument would prove a perfect island exists. what do you do?
options: write a reply, and let both be read with the book.
fork.reveal: Anselm answered Gaunilo, and the objection and the reply are still read with the Proslogion.

original.note: Latin: faith seeking understanding, the title Anselm says he first gave the Proslogion.

trapdoor: what you thought: Anselm is just a name from a list of saints.
what it means: a monk who began from faith and reasoned toward God as that than which nothing greater can be thought.
what a scholar hears: the Proslogion's turn, where God becomes greater than can be thought, and Gaunilo's island in reply.

notes: Proslogion paraphrased: preface (first titled 'Fides quaerens intellectum'), ch. 1 ('I believe in order to understand'), ch. 2 (that than which nothing greater can be thought; the fool), ch. 15 (greater than can be thought). Confirm.
'The two were copied together with the book': Anselm is reported to have asked that Gaunilo's objection and his reply be appended to the Proslogion. Confirm.
'Thomas Aquinas, later, did not accept it as a proof' (Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 1, ad 2); confirm phrasing. 'Philosophers are still arguing about' it is general.
Anselm taught at Bec; his later office as Archbishop of Canterbury and the title's dates are not voiced under the claims rule.
Outline practice is three minutes of thinking about God; the app's sit is two minutes, so the practice invites an optional third minute after the bell.
Original: Latin pronunciation given in ecclesiastical style; confirm.
